body:
Every fact Kiln shows comes from files in the repository, plus git
history and, read-only, Jira. No database, no server: deleting Kiln loses
no information.

From DESIGN.md, goal 1.
title: The repository is the source of truth

body:
The files are Markdown a person can read on GitLab or GitHub, and exports
turn them into a design document where the rest of the organisation
already reads: a Confluence page, a file, a printable HTML page.

From DESIGN.md, goal 2.
title: Readable without Kiln

body:
`kiln check` fails a merge request that breaks a link, duplicates an ID or
leaves an approved requirement unverified.

From DESIGN.md, goal 3.
title: Checkable in CI

body:
Fast enough that nobody waits for it, keyboard-first, with the same
grammar and themes as Fenix and Flint. The budgets are its children and
are requirements, not aspirations.

From DESIGN.md, goal 4.
title: Fast and keyboard-first

body:
No admin rights, a single binary, the system proxy and corporate CA store
honoured, tokens in the OS credential store or CI variables. Headless in a
Linux container.

From DESIGN.md, goal 5.
title: Works on a locked-down corporate machine and in a CI container

body:
Kiln works without Fenix, Flint, Jira or Confluence; each integration
degrades and says so.

From DESIGN.md, goal 6, and INTEGRATION.md, principle 1.
title: No tool requires another

body:
Cold, on a laptop. The benchmark in `crates/kiln-check/examples/bench.rs`
generates such a project and gates CI at 50% over the budget.
title: kiln check on 2,000 items and 50k source files in 2 s

body: At the 95th percentile, re-indexing only the changed file (K4).
title: Language server responds within 50 ms after a keystroke

body: Items are Flint static items, so ordinary typing costs no round trip (K5).
title: Flint provider answers within 16 ms for 2,000 items

body: Excluding diagram rasterisation, which is cached by source hash (K2).
title: Export dry run of a 2,000-item document in 3 s

body:
Every finding has a rule code, a severity and a place, and its message is
one line naming what is wrong and, when it helps, the fix.
title: Findings name the file, line and column

body:
`kiln check` writes GitLab Code Quality reports and GitHub workflow
commands as well as text and JSON, so findings appear on the line that
caused them.
title: Findings show on merge requests

body:
`kiln set`, `link`, `unlink` and `renumber` change only the keys or text
they are about, keep comments and layout, keep the file's line endings,
write atomically, and refuse a file that changed since Kiln read it.
title: Edits keep the author's formatting and never fight an editor

body:
`kiln.toml` is committed, so a key named like a credential is an error
(K004).
title: No secrets in kiln.toml

body:
Two branches can allocate the same number. `kiln check` reports both
files (K101) and `kiln renumber` moves one, rewriting every reference
Kiln counts.
title: Duplicate IDs are found and fixed by one command

body:
A reader who saw the document at a release asks what changed since.
`kiln diff v1.0` lists the items added, removed and changed (status,
title, links, body…), and `kiln export --since v1.0` marks each new or
changed item where it stands and lists them in the changes report.

From DESIGN.md, "Baseline" (K6).
title: Changes since a baseline are shown item by item

body:
Before K12, `kiln gui` (and `kilnw`) found its project by walking up from
the current folder to a `kiln.toml`, and stopped with "no kiln.toml in …
or any folder above it" when there was none. So the window couldn't be
started from a shortcut, the Start menu or Flint without first being in
a project, and looking at a second project meant a second window from a
second folder.

The GUI starts anywhere: outside a project it opens on Home, a picker of
the projects opened before (most recent first) with a way to add another
folder, and inside one `SPC h` goes back to Home to switch to another
project without restarting. The list of projects is the user's, not the
project's, so it is never in a repository. It lives in Kiln's state
folder rather than beside `settings.toml`: its paths are this machine's,
and on Windows the settings roam.

From GUI.md, "Home" (K12).
title: The GUI opens any project from a picker and switches between them

body:
Projects at work write requirements at several levels: what the customer
or the stakeholders need, what the system must do, what each piece of
software must do; for avionics, DO-178C's high- and low-level
requirements. Before K13 Kiln checked one type, `requirement`: a project
could declare a type per level and link them, but nothing checked that a
system requirement answers a stakeholder requirement, or that every
stakeholder requirement was refined, and no report showed the chain from
the top level to the code and tests.

Kiln knows the levels and their order. It reports a requirement that
answers nothing above it unless it is marked derived, one that nothing
below refines, and a link that skips a level. It shows the chains as a
traceability matrix, on the command line and in exports, with the
derived requirements apart, because that is what an assessor asks for. A
project with one level is checked as before.

From FORMAT.md, "Requirement levels" (K13).
title: Requirements at several levels trace to each other, and derived ones say so

body:
Coding agents now implement much of what a design describes, and change
the design too. Without guidance they edit front matter by hand, choose
IDs, write inverse links and edit generated exports: work `kiln check`
then rejects, or worse, accepts and the next export contradicts.

A Kiln project carries a guide that such agents read where they work: how
to read and change the design through Kiln's commands, what they may and
may not decide, and how this project's design is organised (its types,
folders, statuses, links, levels and exports). The organisation part
always matches `kiln.toml`, and CI says when it doesn't; the rules are
the project's to adapt.

From DESIGN.md, "The agent guide" (K14).
title: Coding agents find how this project's design is organised and how to change it

body:
An agent asked to "do the next task" or "implement REQ-014" works from
what Kiln prints. It must be able to read an item whole (its body, not
only its title and links), load the plan in one call it can parse, ask
which work is ready to start, and record what it did (create an item
with its links, tags and body; change tags) in one command each, without
editing front matter by hand. When the plan contradicts itself (a done
milestone with open work, a done task whose dependency isn't), `kiln
check` says so, since an agent moving statuses makes that mistake
quietly.

The agent guide says how the plan is organised and how to work through
it, generated from `kiln.toml` like the rest of its section.

From DESIGN.md, "Milestones", K15.
title: Coding agents read the plan and act on it from the command line

body:
Someone who has never used Kiln, without an agent or Fenix, starts a
project and writes a first requirement and decision. `kiln new` gives
each default type a short body to fill in rather than an empty file;
`kiln export` works straight after `kiln init`; a filter that matches
nothing because it names a status no type has says so instead of
printing nothing; `--open` uses the editor they set; and `kiln --help`
shows the eight everyday commands before the integrations.

From DESIGN.md, "Milestones", K16.
title: A person uses Kiln without an agent: items start with a shape, the first export works, mistakes are said

body:
**Rationale:** after K15 and K16, a person on the GUI and an agent on the command line could see different progress for the same milestone, two agents could take the same task, template prompts could reach the exported document, the default document left the plan out, and a script couldn't tell which JSON shape it was reading.

**Acceptance:** the GUI, `kiln show`, `kiln status` and the roadmap report give one progress per milestone; the GUI marks ready and waiting work as `kiln next` does; `kiln next --unowned` leaves claimed work out; `kiln check` reports template text left in an item past its first status (K215); the `design-doc` export places tasks and tests; every JSON object Kiln prints carries `kiln_json`.

From DESIGN.md, "Milestones", K17.
title: Every view of the plan agrees, and what reaches readers is finished

body:
**Rationale:** a `verifies:` comment counted as verification whether its test passed or not, and a reviewer of a code change had to work out by hand which requirements it touched. At work the trace is evidence; it should say what passed in this run, and a pull request should say which requirements its code changes reach.

**Acceptance:** with `--results` and the CI's JUnit report, `kiln trace` and `kiln check` count a code reference that verifies only when its test passed, and report a failed or missing test (K216, K217); `kiln affected REV` lists the requirements whose implementing or verifying code changed since `REV`, with what to re-check, as text, JSON or CI annotations.

From DESIGN.md, "Milestones", K18.
title: The trace says what passed, and a change says which requirements it touches

body:
**Rationale:** the agent guide leaves sign-off to people, but nothing showed when a status that is someone's call changed, or who changed it. Regulated work asks when a requirement was approved, by whom and in which change; git already knows, and Kiln should say it.

**Acceptance:** `kiln log ID` prints an item's history from git: each commit that changed its status, title, owner, parent, tags, due date or links, with date and author. `kiln signoff REV` lists every sign-off status change since `REV` (requirement approved, decision accepted, risk closed, milestone done by default; `[signoff]` in kiln.toml to change it) with the commit and its author, as text, JSON or CI annotations.

From DESIGN.md, "Milestones", K19.
title: Sign-off is visible: who moved which status, when, in which change

body:
Exported to one Confluence page, a project with several requirement
levels read badly: each level was a chapter of its own, after whatever
types `kiln.toml` declared first, and nothing on the page showed which
system requirement answers which stakeholder requirement except a line
of links under each. Readers at work asked for the requirements as one
tree, on one page, and for each item's facts to be quick to scan.

The document reads top-down: requirements first, as one tree (each
requirement with those of the level below that refine it), then design,
decisions, verification, plan and risks; derived requirements apart.
Every item is in the table of contents, however deep the tree goes, and
each item's facts are a small table whose rows line up from item to
item. Several pages only when the template or the layout says so.

From EXPORT.md, "The requirements tree" (K20).
title: A one-page document reads top-down, its requirements as one tree

body:
Items carry TOML between `+++` lines rather than YAML: Kiln edits front
matter (status, links) and `toml_edit` keeps the author's comments and
layout; TOML is the configuration language of the rest of the suite; and
it has no implicit typing surprises.
title: TOML front matter

body:
IDs are the type's prefix and the next number, readable and said aloud in
meetings, over collision-free IDs nobody can remember. Two branches can
allocate the same number; `kiln check` finds it and `kiln renumber` fixes
it.
title: Sequential IDs, renumbered on collision

body:
Confluence is a published view. Edits made there are detected and
reported as drift, never merged back: the repository stays the one source
(CONFLUENCE.md).
title: One-way publishing to Confluence

body:
The default export is the whole design as one document on one Confluence
page or in one file: one thing to read top to bottom, review and link to,
whose page history is the document's revision history. `sections` and
`tree` split the same document (EXPORT.md).
title: One design document is the default export

body:
`kiln-git` runs the user's `git` rather than linking a git library, as
`fenix-git` does: it already honours their credentials, configuration
and repository format, and CI images have it.
title: Shell out to git

body:
FORMAT.md said "no leading zeros" while every example used three digits.
Found while writing this folder (K1): IDs are written with at least three
digits, zero-padded, and exactly one spelling per number, so `grep` finds
an ID as typed and IDs sort as text up to 999. Another spelling is a
finding that names the right one.
title: One spelling per ID number, at least three digits

body:
A link is a fact in one place, the item it starts from; its inverse
("verified by") is computed. Writing it on the inverse side is a warning
(K109) that says which item to write it in.
title: Links are written once, on their source side

body:
Source files are scanned with the configured regexes over whole text, not
parsed per language. A match inside a string literal counts; in exchange
the scanner works for any language and stays within the check budget.
Kiln's own tests build such text at run time for that reason.
title: Code references are matched on text, not parsed

body:
EXPORT.md wanted a committed Markdown export kept current by
`kiln export --check`, but also had every export name the exported commit
in its summary and link repository files at the last commit that changed
them. A file committed into the repository can't name the commit that
contains it, so the check could never pass. Found while making this
repository's own design document (K2).

A file export inside the repository and not ignored by git is in-tree: it
links repository files with relative paths, which GitLab and GitHub
resolve at the revision being viewed, and its summary names no commit.
Exports outside the repository (Confluence, a file under `target/`) keep
naming commits.
title: Exports kept in the repository name no commit

body:
DESIGN.md planned the Fenix and Flint way for the GUI on Windows: one
GUI-subsystem executable that attaches to the terminal it was typed in,
with `--console` to force one. Fenix and Flint are GUIs first; Kiln is a
command-line and CI tool first, and a GUI-subsystem program isn't waited
for by `cmd.exe` and loses its exit code in batch files, which is what
CI and scripts rely on. Found when the GUI arrived (K7).

`kiln.exe` stays a console program: `kiln` alone or `kiln gui` opens the
window from a terminal. `kilnw.exe`, a GUI-subsystem program next to it,
starts `kiln gui` with no console window: what a shortcut or Flint's
"Open in Kiln" runs. On Linux and macOS there is one `kiln`; `kilnw`
does the same there.
title: kiln stays a console program; kilnw opens the GUI

body:
EXPORT.md planned the `docx` format on the `docx-rs` crate. Building it
(K8) showed that `docx-rs` numbers bookmarks, hyperlinks, pictures and
headers from process-wide counters, so the same document rendered twice
in one `kiln export` comes out with different bytes, and `kiln export
--check` (determinism, EXPORT.md) can't hold. It also pulls in an image
library Kiln doesn't need, and has no notion of a reference document's
styles.

Kiln writes the package itself: WordprocessingML for what the document
tree holds (headings, paragraphs, lists, tables, links, bookmarks,
pictures, a TOC field), in a zip written by the `zip` crate with its
parts in a fixed order and a fixed time. A reference `.docx` is read with
the same crate, and its styles, theme, numbering and page setup are
copied over, with Kiln's missing styles added. About a thousand lines,
every one of them testable as text.

The cost: Kiln owns the subset of the format it writes, and a construct
Word users expect that the tree doesn't have (footnotes, headers and
footers) needs writing by hand. The tree is small and changes rarely, so
that is the cheaper side.
title: Word files are written directly, not through docx-rs

body:
K7 made the GUI a reader: it opened items in Fenix and edited nothing,
leaving `kiln set`, `link`, `new` and `renumber` to the terminal, the
language server and Flint. In use that sent people back to the terminal
for every status change, link and new item, and for every export, plan
and comment check, which is what the window was meant to save them.

From K9 the GUI edits what `kiln set`, `link`, `unlink`, `new` and
`renumber` edit: one-line values (a status, a title, a parent, an owner,
a date), links, new items and IDs. It never edits an item's body: prose
is written in an editor, and Fenix is that editor. Every value is picked
from a list or typed on the footer's single line; there is no text area.

Three things keep the two front doors alike. The checks and the writes
are `kiln-index`'s (`plan_set`, `check_link`, `apply_set`,
`apply_link`, `apply_renumber`, `create_item`), shared with the command
line and the Flint provider, so a value one accepts the others accept and
a file an editor saved in the meantime is refused by all three. Exports
and comments run the commands' own code through the binary, so the
window shows what the terminal prints and never handles a token.
Publishing asks first and publishes only the plan it showed; overriding a
refused plan (`--force`, `--adopt`) and pruning stay on the command
line, where the flag is written down.
title: The GUI edits front matter, never prose

body:
Exports nested items by `parent`: a child was a heading one level below
its parent. Read in Confluence, that hid most requirements from the table
of contents, which stops at three levels (`toc_levels`): a section is
level 1, its items level 2, and every child below that was missing. And
an item's properties were one line (`approved · under REQ-002 · verified
by TEST-031, TEST-032 · implemented by …`), which is compact but hard to
scan once an item has more than two relationships.

Now the items of a `kiln:items` are a flat list of headings at one
level, in tree order, each parent followed by its children, so the
table of contents lists every item and related items still sit
together; the parent shows in the item's properties. `nest="parent"`
keeps the old nesting where a document wants it, and `tree` nests by
default, because there nesting is what makes the page tree. Properties
default to `item_style = "list"`: the status, then one line per
relationship with its label in bold, broken inside one paragraph so the
block stays short. `line` remains for documents that want the compact
form.
title: Items are a flat list, with one line per relationship

body:
Through K8 Kiln only read Jira: a task changed in Kiln left its ticket
behind, and every change was made twice, once in the repository and
once in Jira. K207 noticed the difference but couldn't remove it.

From K10, with `[jira] project` set, `kiln jira sync` keeps Jira in step
with the items, one way, as publishing keeps Confluence in step
(ADR-003). One Jira issue stands for the Kiln project (`[jira] parent`,
created by the first sync), and each synced item, the tasks by default,
is a sub-task of it. Kiln creates those sub-tasks and keeps their
summary, due date and status: the status by the workflow transition that
reaches the mapped status (`[jira.status]`, else Jira's status category).
A ticket created for an item is recorded in the item (`jira = "…"`), and
the project issue in `kiln.toml`, so the commit records the link and no
ticket is ever created twice; a person runs the sync, not CI, for that
reason.

What stays Jira's: assignees, sprints, comments, worklogs, and every
ticket that isn't a sub-task of the project issue, which Kiln never
writes even when an item links it. Kiln deletes nothing: a sub-task no
item links any more is reported. A ticket moved in Jira is flagged by
K207; `kiln jira pull` takes its status back into the item as a
reviewable edit, or the next sync moves it back. The repository stays
the source of truth (REQ-001), and Kiln still holds no assignments or
sprints (RISK-004).
title: Kiln pushes the tasks it manages to Jira

body:
People asked for ready-made documents (arc42 first) that they could add
with one command and then adapt, several to one project.

**Copied, not referenced.** `kiln preset add` writes the template into
the project's `templates/` folder and its configuration into
`kiln.toml`, and from then on all of it is the project's own, changed in
its merge requests; a newer Kiln never touches it. A referenced template
(`template = "preset:arc42"`) would change under its authors with an
upgrade, in the published document of all places, and every team that
adapts arc42 to itself (the normal case) would copy it anyway. The cost
is that improvements to a preset reach only projects that add it
afterwards; `kiln init --preset NAME` in an empty folder writes the
current one to compare with.

**Configuration included, the minimum, nothing twice.** A preset adds
the types and link roles its template places and an export target, so
it works the moment it is added. It adds only what is missing: a type
the project already declares, by hand or from another preset, is kept
as it is; a role it has gains only the `from` and `to` types it lacks;
each preset's export has the preset's name. So `arc42` and `srs` share
`constraint` and `term`, in either order. A prefix clash, a taken export
name or a file already there stops it before anything is written, and
`kiln.toml` is spliced so its comments survive (REQ-013). The links that
go further than the document needs (tests verifying quality scenarios,
code implementing building blocks, blocks using blocks) are choices with
alternatives, so the wiki's "Presets" page offers them to add by hand
rather than the preset making them; a first version that left all
configuration to the wiki made every project paste the same tables.

The presets follow the structure of arc42 and ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 with
wording of Kiln's own, since arc42's help text is CC BY-SA and Kiln is
MIT OR Apache-2.0.
title: Presets are copied into the project and stack without duplicates

body:
Requirements written at several levels needed Kiln to know which types
are levels, in which order, and how a level answers the one above.

**A type per level, ordered in `[requirements] levels`.** Not a `level`
key on each requirement, nor tags: each level has its own prefix
(`SYS-004` says what it is in a meeting), its own statuses and its own
section in the document, which types already give. Declaring the order
once in `kiln.toml` keeps it in one place. Without the table the one
level is `requirement`, so no project changes behaviour.

**`parent` within a level, a link across levels.** `parent` already means
decomposition and makes the tree and the coverage of children; reusing it
across levels would make one requirement's children a mix of finer
system requirements and the software requirements that implement it. A
link role (`refines` by default, `trace` names another) is written once
on the lower side, as every link is (ADR-007), and can point at several
requirements above, which `parent` can't. A requirement with no trace
link traces through its parent, so a decomposed subtree links upward
once.

**Derived requirements are marked, not inferred.** A lower-level
requirement that answers nothing above is either forgotten or
deliberate (DO-178C's derived requirements, which go to the safety
assessment). `derived = true` in front matter is the one way to say
"deliberate"; without it, K208. A key rather than a tag because it
changes what the check does, and tags never do.

**Each rule one fact.** K208 (nothing above), K209 (the wrong level
above), K210 (nothing below), with K201 and K202 applying to every level
their role's `to` names, so a V-model can verify every level and
implement only the lowest. A link that skips a level still counts where
it points: one wrong link is one finding, not two. The levels report
shows the leaf's coverage per chain; each level's own verification is
the traceability report with its `type`, rather than a matrix too wide
to print.
title: Requirement levels are types in order, traced upward by a link; derived ones are marked

body:
A Kiln project needed a guide for coding agents (REQ-019).

**`design/AGENTS.md`, not beside `kiln.toml`.** `kiln.toml` is usually at
the repository root, where `AGENTS.md` is the repository's guide to its
code: not Kiln's to write, and Kiln never overwrites a file. In the
first item folder the guide never collides, sits beside the files it
describes, and is read by agents that honour nested `AGENTS.md` files
when they work there. The cost: an agent working only on the code may not
see it, so the wiki suggests one line in the repository's own guide
pointing at it.

**Two parts.** The rules (use Kiln's commands, link from the source side,
leave sign-off to people…) are written once and are the project's from
then on, like a preset's template (ADR-015): teams differ on what an agent
may approve, and a newer Kiln rewriting their words would be a surprise.
The description of the project (types, folders, statuses, roles, levels,
exports) is generated between two marker lines from `kiln.toml` alone,
because a hand-kept copy goes stale the first time someone adds a type,
and a stale guide misleads an agent more than none. `kiln agents`
rewrites only that section, `kiln preset add` refreshes it, and `kiln
check` warns when it no longer matches (K113), as `kiln export --check`
does for exports. Generating it from the configuration alone, not the
items, keeps it stable across ordinary work and exact to compare.

**Optional.** A project that deletes the section, or the file, has opted
out, and K113 says nothing; a warning by default, since a stale guide
doesn't break the design.
title: The agent guide lives in the design folder, its rules written once and its description generated

body:
K15 adds `kiln next`, which lists the work ready to start (REQ-020).

**Work** is an item of a type the `part-of` role may link from (`task`
by default): what a milestone includes. It is **ready** when it is
neither done nor closed, its status isn't `blocked`, and every item it
`depends-on` is done or closed. Everything else open is **waiting**,
with what it waits on named.

**A milestone groups and orders work, it doesn't gate it.** Work of a
milestone that `depends-on` an unfinished one is still ready when its
own dependencies are: teams overlap milestones, and a gate would hide
the work an agent could pick up. `kiln next` lists the earliest
milestone's work first (open milestones in ID order, work in no
milestone last), so the order the IDs give is the order an agent sees.
The cost: a project that does want a gate writes it, `depends-on` from
the first task of the later milestone to the last of the earlier one.

**`blocked` is a status a person sets, so it is honoured** by name, like
the other default status names some rules know (`verified`,
`superseded`): a project that names it otherwise simply doesn't get
that.

The same definitions feed `kiln status` and the plan checks K211–K214,
so what `next` calls ready is what `check` and `status` agree on.
title: Ready work is open work whose dependencies are finished; milestones group it, they don't gate it

body:
## Context

`kiln new --open` and the GUI's `Enter` opened items in Fenix, else the
operating system's default editor (REQ-021). At work, without Fenix, the
default editor for `.md` on Windows is often Notepad or nothing. People
already name their editor in `VISUAL` or `EDITOR`, and some want Kiln to
use one editor whatever else is installed.

## Decision

The order is `KILN_EDITOR`, the running Fenix, starting Fenix, `VISUAL`,
`EDITOR`, the OS default. `KILN_EDITOR` comes first because the user set
it for Kiln on purpose. `VISUAL` and `EDITOR` come after Fenix because
they are set for every tool, and a Fenix user's shell often sets them to
a terminal editor; putting them first would quietly stop opening Fenix.

A command is split on spaces with quotes, never run through a shell (a
path with `&` stays one argument), and `{path}` and `{line}` are
replaced, the path appended without `{path}`. From the command line the
editor gets the terminal and Kiln waits, as `git commit` does, so `vim`
works; the GUI has no terminal to lend and starts it in the background.

## Consequences

A machine without Fenix opens items where its user expects. A terminal
editor in `KILN_EDITOR` doesn't work from the GUI; the docs say to name a
windowed one there. Kiln still writes nothing of Fenix's.
title: An editor the user names for Kiln comes before Fenix; VISUAL and EDITOR come after it

body:
## Context

Milestone progress counted the work `part-of` a milestone and of every milestone it `depends-on`, transitively. K15's `kiln status` counted only a milestone's own work, so the GUI's Roadmap, the exported roadmap and `kiln show` disagreed with `kiln status` on the same milestone. The wiki already warned that the transitive count misleads whenever `depends-on` only meant the order: in this repository, MS-017 reported K15's tasks as its own.

## Decision

A milestone's progress is its own work: done out of non-closed, over the work `part-of` it directly or through its parent (a sub-task counts where its task does). One function computes it, and `kiln show`, `kiln status`, the GUI and the roadmap report all use it. `depends-on` between milestones orders them and nothing else, as ADR-018 already says for readiness.

## Consequences

Every view shows the same numbers. A project that relied on a later milestone counting the earlier one's work sees smaller totals; it can make the later milestone include that work, or read the earlier milestone's own line. The roadmap report's numbers change for such projects, so their committed exports change once.
title: A milestone's progress is its own work, everywhere

body:
## Context

`--results` reads a JUnit XML report, the format every test runner can write (cargo-nextest, pytest, JUnit, Jest, go-junit-report), and must tell which code reference each test result belongs to. Code references are matched on text, not parsed (ADR-008), so Kiln doesn't know where a test function starts.

## Decision

A `verifies` code reference's test is named by the first declaration after the comment: the name after `fn`, `def`, `func`, `function` or `sub`; else the string in `it("…")`, `test("…")` or `describe("…")`; else the identifier before the first `(`. Attribute and decorator lines (`#[…]`, `@…`) and blank lines are skipped. A JUnit `testcase` matches when its name, or its last `::`, `.` or `/` segment, equals that name; when the report gives a `file`, it must also end with the reference's path. A reference all of whose matches passed counts; one with a failure or error doesn't (K216); one with none, or only skipped ones, didn't run (K217).

## Consequences

It works across languages and runners without a parser, and an explicit name is never needed for the usual layout (the comment on the line before the test). Two tests of the same name in different files share their results unless the report names files; the safer reading wins (any failure is a failure). Without `--results`, nothing changes: a code reference counts as before.
title: Test results are matched to code references by the name of the test that follows them

body:
## Context

`kiln affected` turns a git diff into the requirements it touches. A code reference is a comment on the line before the code it is about, and Kiln doesn't parse code (ADR-008), so where that code ends isn't known.

## Decision

A code reference covers its own line down to the line before the next code reference in the same file, or the end of the file. A changed line inside that range touches the reference's targets; a deletion touches the range it was in. An item file that changed touches that item. Each touched requirement is listed with the changed ranges and the references that reached it, and with what verifies it, to re-check.

## Consequences

It over-reports rather than misses: a reference at the top of a file covers the whole file, which is what a file-level `implements` means. Precision comes from placing references close to their code, which the format already asks for. No language support is needed, and the answer is the same on every machine.
title: A code reference covers the code down to the next one

body:
## Context

The agent guide leaves sign-off (approving a requirement, accepting a decision, closing a risk, finishing a milestone) to people, and K19 makes it visible (REQ-024). Kiln could store approvals in the front matter (`approved_by`, a date), or read them from git.

## Decision

Kiln stores nothing new: git is the record. `kiln log` reads an item's history from `git log --follow` and the file at each commit; `kiln signoff` compares a revision with the working tree and names, for each sign-off status change, the last commit in between that touched the file and its author ("uncommitted" when it isn't committed yet). Which statuses are sign-off is `kiln.toml`'s `[signoff]`, type → statuses, with defaults that follow the guide's rule.

## Consequences

Nothing for an agent to forge in a file and nothing to keep in step; the evidence is as good as the repository's history, and a squash merge credits its author. A shallow clone has less history, which `kiln log` says. Who may sign off stays the repository's protected-branch and review rules: Kiln shows the change, it doesn't block it.
title: Sign-off and history are read from git, never stored in items

body:
ADR-013 made items a flat list and their properties lines of bold
labels, so that a three-level table of contents listed every item and a
short item took little room. With requirement levels (ADR-016) that
left a design document of separate chapters per level and a page where
the relationship readers care most about, which requirement refines
which, showed only as links (REQ-025).

**The requirements tree.** `<!-- kiln:requirements -->`, and the
default layout, place the requirement levels as one tree: each top-level
requirement, the requirements of the level below that refine it one
heading deeper, and so on, then the derived requirements and those that
trace to nothing, each under a heading of their own. Within a level
ADR-013 still holds: a child follows its parent at the same depth, so
the tree is as deep as there are levels, not as deep as the
decomposition. A requirement that refines several is placed under the
first and named, in one line, under the others: a heading in two places
would be two anchors for one item, and Confluence allows one page per
item in `tree`. The table of contents is as deep as the deepest item
(three levels at least, six at most) unless `toc_levels` says, so
ADR-013's reason for flatness holds without the flatness.

**Properties as a table.** Each item's facts are a two-column table
(status first, then relationships, Jira, tags, owner, due) with related
items by ID alone, linked to their heading. Rows line up across items
and an item with five relationships stays five short rows, where the
lines grew long with titles; the title is one click away. The type and
the source file appear only in `tree`, where an item is a page alone;
in a document its section already says both. `list` and `line` remain
for documents read as prose.

**Requirements first.** Without a template, and in the `design-doc`
preset, the requirements come first, then the other types in
`kiln.toml`'s order, so a project that declares its levels last still
reads top-down; `traceability` without `type` is the chain matrix when
there are several levels.
title: Requirements are one tree on the page, and an item's facts are a table
